title: India's Defence Strength
subtitle: Powering National Security through Self-Reliance
body_text:
Strengthening India's Defence
India’s defence sector has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past decade. It has emerged as a stronger, more self-reliant and globally credible force. Guided by Atmanirbhar Bharat, sustained reforms, investment and indigenous innovation have strengthened defence capabilities. The domestic defence industrial base has also expanded significantly. As India marks its 80th Independence Day , this transformation reflects growing confidence in India’s ability to safeguard its sovereignty and contribute to global security.
Defence Investment Strengthening Military Capabilities
3.1-Fold Growth in Defence Budget: The defence budget rose from ₹ 2.53 lakh crore in 2013–14 to ₹ 7.85 lakh crore in 2026–27 . 2.3-Fold Growth in Capital Expenditure: Capital expenditure also increased from ₹ 94,587.95 crore in 2014–15 to ₹ 2.19 lakh crore in 2026–27 , enabling sustained modernisation.
Investment Driving Indigenous Defence Production
Defence production reached a record ₹ 1.78 lakh crore in 2025–26 . 76% production from public-sector entities and 24% from the private sector .
Domestic Industrial Base Expanding Exports
56-Fold Growth in Defence Exports: Exports rose from ₹ 686 crore in FY2013–14 to ₹ 38,424 crore in FY2025–26 . Exports is reaching 80+ countries and increased to over 5,500% in twelve years. Private sector contributed ₹ 17,353 crore or 45.16% of defence exports in FY2025–26, while Defence Public Sector Undertakings contributed ₹ 21,071 crore or 54.84% . The Government targets ₹ 3 lakh crore in annual defence production and ₹ 50,000 crore in exports by 2029 .
Innovation Strengthening Technological Foundation
Defence R&D allocation rose from ₹ 13,716.14 crore in 2014–15 to ₹ 29,100.25 crore in 2026–27 , an increase of over 112% . Since 2022–23, 25% of the defence R&D budget has been opened to industry, start-ups and academia, Testing facilities across 24 DRDO laboratories are accessible through the Defence Testing Portal (DTP), a digital platform managed by the Ministry of Defence. This portal lets domestic manufacturers, startups, and industries request paid access to specialised government testing infrastructure to support indigenous defence production .
Key Initiatives Strengthening India’s Defence Industrial Base
India is expanding its defence industrial capacity through indigenous manufacturing, modern infrastructure and greater private-sector participation. This growing ecosystem is strengthening domestic capabilities, supporting innovation and building a resilient defence supply chain.
Defence Acquisition Reforms
The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) , India’s apex defence procurement body, is driving Atmanirbhar Bharat through indigenous acquisitions. It has accorded Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) for over ₹ 6 lakh crore of DRDO-designed, Indian industry-manufactured systems. Major indigenous acquisitions are strengthening combat capabilities: Approvals include 97 Tejas Mk-1A fighter jets worth ₹ 62,000 crore and 156 LCH Prachand helicopters worth ₹ 62,700 crore . These procurements expand India’s domestic aerospace and defence manufacturing capabilities. Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020 strengthened indigenous procurement and domestic manufacturing. It also expanded opportunities for Indian companies in defence design, development and production. Defence Procurement Procedure (DPP) 2016 streamlined defence acquisitions while advancing Make in India . It laid the foundation for subsequent reforms in defence procurement. Defence Procurement Manual (DPM) 2025 streamlined nearly ₹ 1 lakh crore in revenue procurement. It enabled faster approvals, relaxed penalties for indigenous projects and assured long-term orders.
Draft Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2026 DAP 2026 proposes simpler acquisition categories and stronger support for indigenous design and development. It also proposes indigenous content requirements of up to 60% .
Boosting Innovation — iDEX, ADITI & TDF
The Innovations for Defence Excellence (iDEX ) scheme, with a ₹498.78 crore outlay, engaged 676 startups, MSMEs, and innovators, resulting in 551 design and development contracts as of March 2026. ADITI Scheme: Approved with a ₹750 crore outlay (2023–24 to 2025–26), ADITI provides financial support through the Defence Innovation Organisation (DIO) to accelerate innovative defence technologies. Technology Development Fund: The scheme provides grants of up to ₹ 50 crore for critical defence technology development. As of June 2026, 80 projects worth ₹ 334 crore were under implementation, with an additional ₹ 500 crore corpus sanctioned for deep technology and emerging technologies.
Technology Transfer & Industry Participation
DRDO's Development cum Production Partner framework transferred technologies to 134 partner companies. 2,180 technology transfer agreements signed. 2,780+ IPRs opened for industry use as on March 2026.
Indigenisation & Domestic Manufacturing
Till May 2026, 10 Positive Indigenisation lists, five each of DMA & DDP, covering 5,521 items were notified, resulting in increased Aatmanirbharta in defence production. Srijan Defence Equipment Empowerment Platform (DEEP) is a digital repository promoting indigenous defence sourcing. As of May 2026, it listed over 41,000 vendors and 2.7 lakh products, strengthening domestic supply chains. By April 2026, the Uttar Pradesh Defence Industrial Corridor had attracted ₹ 42,057 crore in investment commitments, with ₹ 4,409 crore grounded . The Tamil Nadu Defence Industrial Corridor attracted ₹ 32,699 crore , with ₹ 6,446 crore realised , strengthening India’s defence manufacturing base. The BrahMos Integration & Testing Facility in Lucknow has begun manufacturing missiles.
Ease of Doing Business & Defence Trade
Industrial licence validity was extended from 7 (+3) years to 15 (+3, up to 18) years, with lifetime validity now granted under the Arms Act. The revamped Defence Exim Portal enables end to end application processing, automated company verification, simplified registration, real time tracking and secure payment integration, making defence trade clear and more efficient. The FDI limit in the defence sector was increased to 74% under the Automatic Route and up to 100% via the Government Route, attracting ₹6,670.59 crore in inflows by March 2026.
The reforms have created a more enabling environment for defence manufacturing, with stronger institutional support and clearer pathways from innovation to deployment.
Advancing India’s Defence Self-Reliance: FY 2025–26
India’s defence landscape has undergone a significant shift towards greater domestic capability, technological sophistication and operational resilience. Indigenous development now spans ammunition, missiles, propulsion, air defence and naval platforms, supported by stronger government-industry collaboration. Indigenisation Strengthening Operational Self-Reliance
The Indian Army achieved roughly 91% self-sufficiency by indigenising 159 out of 175 ammunition variants in its inventory. India has successfully tested the Agni-4 Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile and Agni-5 Long Range Surface-to-Surface Ballistic Missile , validating their operational and technical parameters. The TARA Glide Weapon and RudraM-II air-to-surface missile have also demonstrated indigenous precision-strike capabilities against ground targets. The DRDO has advanced multiple indigenous systems, including the Kusha Long Range Air Defence Missile and Very Short-Range Air Defence System (VSHORADS) . An integrated air-defence system combining missile interceptors, short-range weapons and laser technologies has also been successfully tested.
DRDO successfully conducted a 12-minute ground test of an actively cooled scramjet combustor , supporting hypersonic missile development.
Advancing Maritime Defence And Strike Capabilities
The Indian Navy commissioned 12 warships and submarines , including INS Surat, INS Nilgiri and INS Vaghsheer . INS Mahendragiri , stealth frigate, also entered service with over 75% indigenous content . SHACHI , the first of 11 Next Generation Offshore Patrol Vessels , launched. INS Dunagiri, INS Sanshodhak and INS Agray also commissioned, completing the indigenous Sandhayak-class survey fleet , expanding maritime surveillance and survey capabilities. DRDO successfully tested the Naval Anti-Ship Missile–Medium Range and demonstrated multi-layered Ballistic Missile Defence capability. It is strengthening India’s ability to counter diverse aerial and maritime threats.
India’s defence transformation has built greater depth across military preparedness, manufacturing and internal security.
Powering India’s Defence Ambition to 2047
India’s defence transformation reflects a clear shift towards greater self-reliance, technological capability and global confidence. Stronger indigenous production, research and development, innovation and industry participation are enhancing defence capacity across land, air and maritime domains. Growing exports and strategic partnerships are reinforcing India’s role as a reliable global defence partner. With continued investment in advanced technologies and domestic manufacturing, India is building the capabilities needed to meet future security requirements and strengthen its position as a technologically advanced defence power by 2047.

enrichment.summary: This Independence Day backgrounder from the Ministry of Defence summarises a decade of reforms under Atmanirbhar Bharat, citing a 3.1-fold rise in the defence budget (₹2.53 lakh crore in 2013-14 to ₹7.85 lakh crore in 2026-27), record indigenous defence production of ₹1.78 lakh crore in 2025-26, and a 56-fold jump in defence exports (₹686 crore to ₹38,424 crore) reaching 80+ countries. It also lists key institutional reforms (DAP 2020, DPM 2025, draft DAP 2026), innovation schemes (iDEX, ADITI, TDF), indigenisation platforms (Positive Indigenisation Lists, SRIJAN-DEEP), defence corridors in UP and Tamil Nadu, and major indigenous platforms such as Tejas Mk-1A, LCH Prachand, Agni-4/5, and several Navy warships. Government targets are ₹3 lakh crore in annual production and ₹50,000 crore in exports by 2029.
enrichment.context:
India's defence self-reliance push traces back to the 2001 opening of defence production to the private sector, but gained momentum after 2014 with 'Make in India' and later 'Atmanirbhar Bharat', particularly following the 2020 border tensions with China which exposed import dependence. Key milestones include the Defence Procurement Procedure (DPP) 2016, its replacement by the Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020, and the raising of FDI limits (49% to 74% automatic route in 2020). Institutions like the Defence Acquisition Council, DRDO, and the Defence Innovation Organisation (running iDEX and ADITI) are central to this ecosystem, while DPSUs (like HAL, BEL, Mazagon Dock) and a growing private sector (Tata Advanced Systems, Bharat Forge, Adani Defence) now co-produce major platforms.

This matters for UPSC because indigenisation and defence exports are recurring themes in GS Paper 3 (science & technology, economy) and GS Paper 2/3 (internal/external security), especially given India's stated ambition to become a top-25 global defence exporter and its evolving strategic partnerships (QUAD, France, Russia diversification). The mention of platforms like Agni-5, BrahMos, Tejas Mk-1A, and INS Vaghsheer connects to India's nuclear deterrence, missile technology, and naval modernisation debates, while indigenisation lists and defence corridors relate to Make in India's industrial policy dimension.

prelims_questions.question:
Consider the following statements regarding India's defence sector reforms as of 2026:
1. The FDI limit in defence under the Automatic Route is 74%.
2. The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) is India's apex defence procurement body.
3. The iDEX scheme is administered directly by the Ministry of Finance.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
prelims_questions.explanation: The release confirms FDI up to 74% via Automatic Route and that DAC is the apex procurement body. iDEX is run through the Defence Innovation Organisation (DIO) under the Ministry of Defence, not the Ministry of Finance, so statement 3 is incorrect.

prelims_questions.question: The 'Positive Indigenisation Lists' mentioned in India's defence self-reliance drive are notified by which entities?
options: Department of Defence Production (DDP) and Department of Military Affairs (DMA)
Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Finance
Defence Acquisition Council and Indian Navy
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states that 10 Positive Indigenisation Lists, five each from the Department of Military Affairs (DMA) and Department of Defence Production (DDP), have been notified, covering 5,521 items.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of indigenisation initiatives such as the Positive Indigenisation Lists, iDEX, and Defence Industrial Corridors in achieving India's goal of 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' in defence production. What challenges remain in scaling up private sector participation?
mains_questions.gs_paper: GS Paper 3 - Economy and Science & Technology: Defence Indigenisation

mains_questions.question: India's defence exports have grown significantly over the past decade. Examine the factors driving this growth and assess its implications for India's strategic partnerships and standing as a global defence supplier.
mains_questions.gs_paper: GS Paper 2/3 - International Relations and Economy: Defence Exports and Strategic Autonomy

study_notes.reason: The release combines a dense set of testable facts — scheme names, procurement documents, FDI limits, indigenisation platforms and specific weapons systems — with a genuine analytical narrative on India's shift toward strategic autonomy in defence and its emergence as an arms exporter, so neither the factual nor the analytical half can be called secondary.

prelims.point: Evolution of defence procurement frameworks: DPP 2016 → DAP 2020 → DPM 2025 → draft DAP 2026 (each with distinct focus: streamlining, indigenous procurement, revenue procurement/faster approvals, indigenous content up to 60%)
prelims.why_important: UPSC often tests the correct sequence and distinguishing feature of successive policy documents rather than their content alone.

prelims.point: Innovation schemes: iDEX (₹498.78 crore outlay, startups/MSMEs), ADITI (₹750 crore, via Defence Innovation Organisation), Technology Development Fund (grants up to ₹50 crore)
prelims.why_important: These are distinct named schemes with different implementing bodies and funding ceilings that could be mixed up in a matching-type question.

prelims.point: FDI limit in defence: 74% under Automatic Route, up to 100% via Government Route
prelims.why_important: This is a frequently tested factual threshold showing India's liberalisation of a strategic sector and is easy to confuse with other sector-specific FDI caps.

prelims.point: Positive Indigenisation Lists (10 lists, 5,521 items, jointly by DMA and DDP) and SRIJAN-DEEP as a vendor/product digital repository
prelims.why_important: Positive Indigenisation Lists are a recurring current-affairs mechanism for import substitution that UPSC could ask about directly.

mains.point: Indigenisation drive (91% ammunition self-sufficiency, indigenous content in warships, Positive Indigenisation Lists) reflects a strategic shift toward reducing import dependence exposed by border tensions and geopolitical volatility
mains.analytical_use: Useful for questions on how Atmanirbhar Bharat strengthens national security and reduces vulnerability to supply-chain disruptions from foreign suppliers.

mains.point: Growing private-sector share in defence production (24%) and exports (45%) signals a structural shift from a purely DPSU-dominated model to public-private co-production
mains.analytical_use: Can be deployed in questions on the changing structure of India's defence-industrial base and challenges of integrating private players with DPSUs and DRDO.

mains.point: 56-fold rise in defence exports to 80+ countries positions India as an emerging defence supplier, reinforcing strategic partnerships and soft power alongside 'Make in India'
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on India's evolving role in global defence trade and its use as a tool of foreign policy leverage with partner countries.

both.concept: Government targets of ₹3 lakh crore annual defence production and ₹50,000 crore exports by 2029, alongside record 2025-26 figures
both.prelims_angle: UPSC could test the specific target figures and the base year/production figures for 2025-26
both.mains_angle: Enables discussion of whether current growth trajectory is sustainable and what structural gaps (R&D depth, critical component imports, technology transfer bottlenecks) must be addressed to meet these targets

low_priority.point: Framing around India's 80th Independence Day and rhetorical statements about 'growing confidence' and 'global credibility'
low_priority.reason: Ceremonial language with no testable content or independent analytical value.

low_priority.point: FDI inflow figure of ₹6,670.59 crore by March 2026
low_priority.reason: An isolated statistic without benchmark or trend comparison, unlikely to be tested on its own.

low_priority.point: Mention that BrahMos Integration and Testing Facility in Lucknow has 'begun manufacturing missiles'
low_priority.reason: A single-line operational update without further detail or significance attached.
